lesson.text: Quick memory: in 'Energy on the move', what does a lamp change electricity into? (Light.) Now build electric circuits yourself, and learn how to stay safe with electricity.

Electricity powers lamps, fridges and phones. Mains electricity comes from sockets in the wall: it is strong enough to badly hurt you, so never play with plugs or sockets. Batteries are much weaker and safe to experiment with.
A circuit is a complete loop. Electricity flows out of the battery, along a wire, through the bulb and back to the battery. A battery's proper name is a cell, and it has a + end and a − end.
If there is a gap anywhere in the loop, the electricity stops and the bulb goes out. A switch is a gap you can open and close: closed, the loop is complete and the bulb lights; open, it goes out.

Conductors let electricity flow through them: metals such as copper, iron, steel, aluminium and gold. Insulators do not: plastic, rubber, wood, glass, paper and cloth. Wires are copper inside a plastic coat.

To test a material, lay it across a gap in the loop. A steel spoon lights the bulb: it is a conductor. A rubber eraser leaves it dark: an insulator. Water can conduct too, so keep electrical things away from water and wet hands.
On this unit's page, tap TRY IT IN THE LAB: close the switch, then take out a wire to make a gap. Add a second bulb: two bulbs in one loop share the battery's push, so both glow more dimly.
Try it in the world: in your world, join a lever to a lamp and flip it on and off, just like a switch in a circuit. Next, in grade 5: circuits drawn with symbols, and circuits with two paths.

exercises.prompt: What is an electric circuit?
exercises.hint: Think of the path from the battery and back again.
exercises.explain: A circuit is a complete loop: from the battery, through the wires and the bulb, and back.
choices: a complete loop that electricity flows round

exercises.prompt: In this circuit the switch is open, so the bulb lights up.
exercises.hint: What does an open switch make in the loop?
exercises.explain: False: an open switch is a gap, so the loop is broken and the bulb stays off.

exercises.prompt: Which of these is a conductor of electricity?
exercises.hint: Which one is made of metal?
exercises.explain: Copper is a metal, and metals let electricity through.

exercises.prompt: Which of these is an insulator?
exercises.hint: Insulators are not metals.
exercises.explain: Plastic does not let electricity through: an insulator. Steel, iron and aluminium are metals: conductors.

exercises.prompt: What is the right thing to do with a plug socket?
exercises.hint: Mains electricity is strong enough to badly hurt you.
exercises.explain: Never play with sockets: the electricity in the walls can badly hurt you. Experiment only with small batteries.
choices: leave it alone and ask a grown-up

exercises.prompt: Sort them: do they run on mains electricity or on batteries?
exercises.hint: Could you carry it around? Things you carry often run on batteries.
exercises.explain: Mains: the fridge, the washing machine and the cooker. Batteries: the torch, the watch and the remote.

exercises.prompt: Why does this bulb not light?
exercises.hint: Follow the wire all the way round. Is it joined everywhere?
exercises.explain: The bottom wire has a gap, so the loop is broken and no electricity can flow.
choices: There is a gap in the loop.
The wires are made of copper.

exercises.prompt: Put the path of the electricity in order, starting at the battery.
exercises.hint: Electricity goes out of the battery, round the loop and back.
exercises.explain: Out of the + end, along the wire, through the bulb and back to the − end: a complete loop.
items: along a wire to the bulb
along a wire back to the battery's − end

exercises.prompt: Why are wires made of copper with a plastic coat?
exercises.hint: Which part lets electricity through, and which part is safe to touch?
exercises.explain: Copper is a good conductor, so electricity flows along it. The plastic coat is an insulator, so it keeps the electricity in.
choices: Copper conducts; the plastic keeps us safe.

exercises.prompt: Two bulbs in one loop glow more brightly than one bulb on its own.
exercises.hint: Remember the Lab: what happened when you added a second bulb?
exercises.explain: False: two bulbs share the battery's push, so each glows more dimly.

exercises.prompt: What does a switch do in a circuit?
exercises.hint: Think of what happens when you press a light switch.
exercises.explain: A switch opens a gap (off) or closes it (on), so it breaks or completes the loop.
choices: It opens and closes a gap in the loop.

exercises.prompt: Match each part of a circuit to its job.
exercises.hint: Which part gives the push, and which parts use the electricity or control it?
exercises.explain: The cell pushes electricity round, the wire carries it, the bulb gives out light, the switch opens and closes the loop, and the buzzer makes a sound.

exercises.prompt: In this circuit, the buzzer buzzes.
exercises.hint: Is the loop complete, and is the switch closed?
exercises.explain: True: the loop is complete and the switch is closed, so electricity flows and the buzzer buzzes.

exercises.prompt: Tilly lays a rubber eraser across the gap. What will happen?
exercises.hint: Is rubber a metal?
exercises.explain: Rubber is an insulator: it does not let electricity through, so the gap stays open and the bulb stays off.
choices: The bulb stays off: rubber is an insulator.
The bulb lights: rubber is a conductor.
The bulb lights, but only for a second.
The bulb glows more brightly than before.

exercises.prompt: Bram's loop is complete and his switch is closed, but the bulb does not light. What could be wrong?
exercises.hint: Everything is joined. What gives the push?
exercises.explain: If the loop is complete and the switch is closed, the battery may be flat: used up, with no push left. A new battery would light the bulb.
choices: The bulb is in the loop.

exercises.prompt: Water can conduct electricity, so electrical things must be kept away from water.
exercises.hint: Why are plug sockets kept away from baths and sinks?
exercises.explain: True: water can carry electricity, which is why sockets are kept away from sinks and baths.

exercises.prompt: Zara wants a torch that she can turn off. What must she add to her circuit?
exercises.hint: What opens and closes the loop?
exercises.explain: A switch lets her open the loop (off) and close it again (on).

exercises.prompt: Sort them: conductors or insulators of electricity?
exercises.hint: Test each one in your head: would it light the bulb across the gap? Only the metals do.
exercises.explain: Conductors: the foil, the gold ring and the brass key (all metals). Insulators: the glass marble, the china cup and the cork.

exercises.prompt: Order the steps to test whether a material conducts electricity.
items: Make a gap in the loop.
Lay the material across the gap.
Build a loop with a battery and a bulb.
exercises.hint: Build a working circuit first, then make the gap for the test.
exercises.explain: Build a loop with a battery and a bulb, make a gap in it, lay the material across the gap, and watch: if the bulb lights, the material conducts.

exercises.prompt: Match each thing you notice to its cause.
items: a complete loop, but no light
the wire is safe to hold
exercises.hint: Think about the battery's push, sharing it, gaps, and insulators.
exercises.explain: A complete loop with no light: the battery is flat. Two dim bulbs: they share the battery's push. A bulb that suddenly goes out: the switch was opened. A wire safe to hold: its plastic coat insulates.

play.hook: The lamp on the workbench is dark. Find out what a circuit needs to make it shine!
coach: A circuit is a complete loop.
A gap anywhere stops the electricity.
A switch is a gap you can open and close.
Metals conduct; plastic, rubber and wood do not.
Keep electrical things away from water.
play.world_task: In your world, join a lever to a lamp and flip it on and off, just like a switch.
